name: microservices
context: Large-scale distributed systems requiring independent deployability and scaling. Structures an application as a collection of small, independently deployable services that communicate via lightweight mechanisms (RESTful APIs, message queues, or event-driven channels). Each service owns its data and can be developed, tested, and deployed independently.
benefits: Independent scaling: Scale services based on their specific load patterns without scaling entire applications
Technology diversity: Each service can use different tech stacks, languages, and databases
Fault isolation: Failure in one service doesn't cascade to other services
Team autonomy: Teams own services end-to-end from development to deployment
Deployment independence: Deploy services without coordinating with other teams
Focused maintainability: Teams can focus on isolated updates without impacting entire system
Polyglot persistence: Select optimal database technology per service's specific needs
tradeoffs: Distributed system complexity: Network calls introduce latency, partial failures, and retry logic requirements
Data consistency challenges: Eventual consistency replaces ACID transactions; saga orchestration needed
Operational overhead: More services to monitor, deploy, manage, and secure
Testing complexity: Integration and end-to-end testing across service boundaries
Debugging difficulty: Distributed tracing required to track requests across services
Increased infrastructure cost: More compute, storage, and networking resources
Network latency: Inter-service communication adds response time overhead
Team coordination complexity: API contracts must be carefully managed
use_cases: Multiple teams (10+) working independently on different business domains
Independent service scaling based on heterogeneous load patterns
Various technology stacks required across different services
Frequent deployment of individual services with CI/CD pipelines
Building platforms or ecosystems requiring extensibility
Organizations with mature DevOps practices and observability culture
avoid_when: Small teams with simple requirements and limited expertise
Strong consistency (ACID) requirements where transactions span services
Low-latency use cases requiring sub-millisecond response times
Simple domain with straightforward workflows and predictable load
Projects with limited infrastructure and operational capabilities
Tight deadlines where microservices complexity would slow delivery
component_types: API Gateway: Entry point handling auth, routing, rate limiting, and request aggregation
Service Registry: Database of available service instances with health checks
Service Discovery: Dynamic location of service instances (DNS-based or agent-based)
Configuration Server: Centralized externalized configuration management
Service Mesh: Service-to-service communication with mTLS, observability, and traffic management
Message Broker: Asynchronous communication (Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS)
Centralized Logging: Log aggregation from all services (ELK, Loki, CloudWatch)
Distributed Tracing: Request tracking across service boundaries (Jaeger, Zipkin, X-Ray)
anti_patterns: Distributed monolith: Services separated technically but logically intertwined with synchronous dependencies
Shared database: Multiple services directly accessing same database, defeating independence
Chatty services: Excessive synchronous calls between services causing latency
God services: Services that do too much, violating single responsibility principle
Fallback fallacy: Ignoring circuit breaker patterns leading to cascade failures
Shared libraries with domain logic: Creating coupling through common code sharing
Timeout ignorance: Missing timeouts causing thread pool exhaustion
Observability neglect: Distributed tracing without correlation IDs
design_principles: Single Responsibility: Each service does one thing well, aligned with bounded contexts or business capabilities
Independent Deployment: Services can be deployed without coordinating with other teams
Decentralized Data: Each service owns its database, enabling polyglot persistence
Smart Endpoints: Services contain business logic; pipes only transport data
Infrastructure Automation: Automated testing and deployment through CI/CD pipelines
Observability: Comprehensive logging, metrics, and distributed tracing across service boundaries
Resilience: Design for failure with circuit breakers, retries, and bulkheads
API Contracts: Stable interfaces between services enabling independent evolution
best_practices: Service Decomposition: Design services around business capabilities using domain-driven design
Database per Service: Never share databases between services; maintain strict schema isolation
Asynchronous Communication: Prefer async messaging to reduce coupling and improve resilience
Circuit Breakers: Implement circuit breaker pattern to prevent cascade failures
Distributed Tracing: Add correlation IDs to track requests across service boundaries
Configuration Management: Externalize all configuration; never hardcode environment-specific values
Health Checks: Implement liveness and readiness probes for each service
Graceful Degradation: Design services to degrade gracefully when dependencies fail
Service Mesh: Use service mesh for standardized mTLS, traffic management, and observability
API Versioning: Version APIs from the start to enable independent service evolution
